transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I can’t get past how rough and worn my face and hands look. The cracks, the spots, the sagging—it feels like every banker or county person I deal with is staring at it. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, but it bothers me a lot.
Do you believe there is something genuinely wrong or ugly about how your face or hands look?

Yes, I do. My face looks rough and sagging to me, and my hands have all these cracks and spots. When I’m dealing with bankers or county people, I feel like that’s what they see first—that I look worn-out and ugly. My wife says it’s just from working outdoors, but I can’t really see it that way.
Do you spend a lot of time checking, hiding, or trying to fix how your face or hands look?

Yeah. Before a loan meeting or when I’m setting up at a craft fair, I’ll check myself in the truck mirror and the bathroom mirror over and over. I keep adjusting my hat, trying to see if it hides things, and I compare my hands to the younger workers’. It can eat up time I ought to be spending on the farm.
Do you ever avoid meeting with bankers, county officials, or going to craft fairs because you’re worried people will judge how your face or hands look?

Yes. I’ve missed calls with bankers and put off farm decisions because I couldn’t get myself looking acceptable enough to sit down with people. And I’ve stopped agreeing to photos that could help promote the retreat and the craft sales.
Is your fear of being judged by other people mainly because of how your face and hands look?

Yes. That’s the main thing. I feel like they’re looking at the sagging in my face and the cracks and spots on my hands, like it makes me look worn-out or ugly. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors, but I can’t get past how it looks to other people.
Do unwanted thoughts about how your face or hands look keep popping into your mind even when you try not to think about them?

Yes. I try to put it out of my mind, but it keeps coming back—how rough my face looks, the sagging, and the cracks and spots on my hands. I keep thinking people, especially bankers or county folks, are staring at it, even though my wife tells me I just look like I’ve worked outdoors.
Do other people generally say that the problems you see in your face and hands are minor or not really noticeable?
My wife does. She tells me it’s not that noticeable, that I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors. But I don’t see it that way—I feel like the cracks, spots, and sagging stand out to everybody.
Do most other people besides your wife also seem to think your face and hands look normal or only slightly worn, rather than noticeably ugly or deformed?
I don’t know what most people really think. My wife says it’s just weathered from outdoor work, but I still feel like bankers and county people notice the cracks, spots, and sagging right away.
If you looked exactly the way you wanted, would you still feel very anxious about meeting with bankers, county officials, or being at craft fairs?

I think I’d be a lot less anxious. I’ve missed calls with bankers and put off farm decisions because I couldn’t get myself looking acceptable enough to sit down with people. And I’ve stopped agreeing to photos that could help promote the retreat and the craft sales.
Do you think you might be exaggerating how bad your face and hands look, or are you certain they really do look ugly or deformed?

I know my wife says I’m seeing it worse than it is, but I’m not convinced. To me, my face and hands look rough and worn down, and I feel like people—especially bankers or county folks—notice the cracks, spots, and sagging right away.
Are you absolutely certain that your face and hands look ugly or deformed?

I’m not absolutely certain, no. My wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outdoors. But when I see the cracks, spots, and sagging, it feels pretty hard to believe other people aren’t staring at it—especially bankers or county people.
When you check mirrors or adjust your hat, does it mainly make the thoughts about your face and hands feel less intense for a little while?

Yes, for a little while. Before a loan meeting or setting up at a craft fair, I’ll keep checking the bathroom mirror or the truck mirror, adjusting my hat over and over. I compare my hands to the younger workers’ hands too. It settles me briefly, but I end up wasting time I ought to be using on the farm.
Do you have other repetitive thoughts or rituals that are not about how your face or hands look?
Not that I’ve noticed. Mostly it’s the checking and worrying about my face and hands.
Are you also afraid that people will judge you for things other than your face or hands?
I’m not sure what you mean exactly. The thing that gets to me is how my face and hands look. That’s what I figure people notice.
When people might judge you for reasons other than how your face or hands look, do you still get very anxious?
I don’t think so, not in the same way. If I’m worried, it usually comes back to my face or my hands and how they look to people.
Besides checking mirrors, do you find yourself repeatedly comparing how your face or hands look to other people's?

Yeah, I do. Before I go to a loan meeting or set up at a craft fair, I’ll look at myself in the truck mirror and the bathroom mirror, keep turning my hat around, and compare my hands to the younger workers’. It can eat up time I should be spending on the farm.
About how much time each day do you spend thinking about how your face and hands look?

A few hours, most days, if I’m honest. It’s the roughness in my face and the spots, and my hands looking cracked and worn. I keep thinking everybody—bankers, county people—is staring at it, even though my wife says I just look like a man who’s worked outside.
Do these thoughts about your face and hands feel intrusive and unwanted?

Yeah. I don’t want to keep thinking about it, but it just comes up—how rough my face looks, the spots, my hands all cracked and worn. Then I’m sure the banker or county folks are looking at it, even when my wife tells me it’s just from working outdoors.
Do you worry that your face and hands look abnormal to other people?

Yes. I worry they see the cracks and spots, and how sagging and worn my face looks. It feels like the banker or county people are staring at it, even though my wife says I just look like I’ve worked outdoors.
Has a doctor or dermatologist told you that the cracks, spots, or sagging on your face and hands are minor or just normal weathering from outdoor work?
No, not a doctor. My wife keeps saying it’s just from being outdoors and working, but I can’t get past how rough and worn it looks.

Insight is not absent/delusional because he is not absolutely certain.
